abstract: |
  A scientific study passes through many hands, each working with a different artifact. The study moves from the researcher to the ethics committee and the participant, then on to the software engineer, the analyst, the reviewer, and the replicator. The artifact changes at each step: a protocol PDF and an experiment script become a dataset and a preprocessing notebook, then a manuscript figure and a CONSORT diagram. Because these artifacts drift apart, no single representation describes the study as it was actually run. Cognitive science has almost standardized the data; the process that produces the data is still left to prose and code. We set out the desiderata a specification language must meet to close this gap, and present *Studyflow*, a framework that meets them. At its core a study is a typed directed graph, implemented as an extension of Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) with elements specific to experimental cognitive science: domain-specific activities (cognitive task, questionnaire, instruction), decision gateways (randomization, eligibility), data operations (map, filter, reduce), and data elements bound to community standards. A single Studyflow file is at once the protocol, the specification, the publication figure, and the participant-facing application. We describe the notation, the multiple views it projects for different audiences, and an open-source reference toolkit (a modeler and a runner) built on top of it. To demonstrate the framework end to end, we follow one study from protocol design to publication: a randomized controlled trial in which human participants and a cohort of artificial agents perform a battery of six cognitive tasks, all run from one file. Their responses show where people and agents agree across the six tasks and where they diverge.

# 1. Introduction

## 1.1 The reproducibility gap is in *processes*, not just data

A scientific study touches many people and systems. A researcher designs it; an ethics committee approves it; a participant runs it; a data pipeline ingests it; a model trains on it; a reviewer reads it as a manuscript; and a replicator tries to rebuild it. Reproducing it later requires more than the data and the manuscript: it requires an explicit, complete description of the *processes* that generated them [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines]. A complete description of any computing system needs both a data model (for its structure) and a process model (for its behavior) [@olive2007conceptual]. In cognitive sciences, however, standardization has focused on the data, so the processes behind it are documented only in narrative prose, ad-hoc lab conventions, box-and-arrow diagrams, or code repositories that drift from the text they accompany [@bell2021perspectives; @osc2015]. The community has strong standards for the data plane, notably BIDS and Psych-DS; the process plane, a machine-readable record of how those data came to be, has no equivalent. That asymmetry is the gap this paper addresses, rather than any shortage of data standards.

The cost of this missing process model is clearest when someone other than the author re-reads a study, and largest in neuroscience and clinical research, where one study may record EEG, fMRI, eye tracking, and behavior, pass through an ethics board and a trial registry, and end in a CONSORT diagram. The researcher's protocol PDF, the ethics application, the experiment script, the preprocessing notebook, the model card, the manuscript figure, and the CONSORT diagram all begin as different views of the same study, and they end as inconsistent ones. By that point, no single artifact describes the study *as it was actually run*. Reviewers and replicators reach the code and data through these artifacts, so divergence among the artifacts limits how far the code and data can be independently checked. Trust in research is built or lost here.

The usual way to compensate for a missing process model is voluntary narrative reporting: checklists, pre-registration forms, and journal endorsements. The available evidence suggests it has limited effect. A cross-sectional study of 400 psychology articles published in 2022 found that 7-14% had been preregistered and 14-16% shared raw data, despite more than a decade of data sharing and reproducibility reform [@hardwicke2024prevalence], and gaps between endorsement and adherence recur across fields and journal policies [@percie2020arrive; @hair2019iicarus; @hardwicke2024transparency]. The reason is structural rather than a matter of researcher compliance: a checklist records *what to mention* without requiring *what to share*, and it accepts a narrative description of a process in place of a formal, verifiable one. Consequently, the underlying process model stays implicit and open to interpretation.

We argue that reproducibility should be a property of the shared artifact itself, rather than separate documentation kept alongside the work. A single representation that is machine-readable, human-understandable, and shared across a study's many audiences would keep the process model and the data model aligned. This paper's contribution is one concrete version of that idea, built on a standard process notation and a working open-source toolkit that can be replaced without losing the underlying specification.

## 1.2 Related work

Today each audience works with a different artifact, and these are hard to keep consistent. Existing approaches fall into a few overlapping families, none of which represents the whole study as one shared, executable artifact.

**Workflow engines and pipelines.** Scientists have long automated analysis with custom scripts or domain pipelines, and graphical platforms lowered the barrier to composing them: Galaxy [@thegalaxycommunity2024] and KNIME [@berthold2009] for general analysis, PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy], jsPsych, and lab.js for behavioral tasks, and Taverna and Kepler in early scientific computing. Modern engines model a process as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks and orchestrate execution on clusters and the cloud, among them Apache Airflow, Luigi, Pegasus, Nextflow [@nextflow], and Kedro [@kedro], with NiPype and Pydra [@pydra] serving neuroimaging; workflow domain-specific languages such as the Common Workflow Language [@cwl] and the Workflow Description Language make pipelines portable and declarative, and a long tail of lighter and HPC-oriented engines (Snakemake [@wirth2024], Viash [@cannoodt2024], excitingtools [@buccheri2023], Funsies [@lavigne2021], Caliban [@ritchie2020], Jobflow [@rosen2024], Pipengine [@strozzi2017], Executorlib [@janssen2025], Mantik [@seidler2024], kiwiPy [@uhrin2020]) and workflows-as-a-service or monitoring layers such as DARE [@klampanos2020] and Autosubmit [@uruchi2021] push reproducible execution at scale [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows]. Closer to the bench, reproducibility-oriented analysis toolkits wrap statistics and modeling into shareable, publishing-ready units, among them the Psycho package [@makowski2018], BayesFlow for amortized Bayesian workflows [@radev2023], AnyPyTools [@lund2019], and Yellowbrick [@bengfort2019]. These systems are powerful, but their representations target machines and developers, model the workflow as a DAG suited to fixed-input data pipelines, and encode study logic in code and configuration, as do continuous-integration tools such as GitHub Actions [@kinsman2021] repurposed for analysis. They demand programming skills that ethics boards, reviewers, and many other collaborators do not have.

**Protocol registries and reporting standards.** Experimental protocols are shared as free text through registries such as protocols.io [@teytelman2016] or as manuscript supplements, and the EQUATOR network [@simera2010equator] catalogs reporting guidelines: CONSORT for randomized trials [@hopewell2025consort; @moher2012], SPIRIT for protocols [@spirit2013; @chan2025spirit], STROBE [@strobe], STARD [@stard], PRISMA [@page2021prisma], and TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier], several of which standardize a study-flow diagram [@egger2001]. These enforce structure only at the reporting stage, store it in free-form fields and proprietary formats such as PDF or DOCX, and yield no executable or machine-checkable model of the procedure.

**Data standards and ontologies.** Community standards prescribe how datasets are organized: BIDS [@bids] and its EEG extension [@pernet2019eegbids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW [@csvw], our own Behaverse Data Model [@bdm], and the FAIR principles [@fair]. Adjacent efforts structure analysis outputs and methods reporting, NIDM-Results [@maumet2016nidm] and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis], and process ontologies formalize procedure semantics [@norouzi2025semantic_processes]. All make the data or its products machine-readable but say little about the process that produced them, and ontologies in particular carry high upfront cost and see low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

**Provenance and process tracking.** Provenance systems and data-lifecycle tools such as Science Capsule [@ghoshal2021] record which software produced which output [@souza2020provenance], and process mining recovers models from runtime traces [@vanderaalst2016process]. They track the computational graph well but rarely the experimental context, eligibility decisions, randomization, manual annotations such as ICA labeling, and protocol deviations [@simmons2018provenance_sport], leaving a boundary between a well-tracked computational graph and a partially represented experimental one.

**Visual notations and process modeling.** Box-and-arrow figures communicate study logic at a glance but are not always standardized, not machine-verifiable, and rarely connected to the code, each tailored to one stakeholder: a CONSORT flow for a journal, a slide deck for a funding agency, a whiteboard sketch for an engineer [@bogale2024]. Standardized graphical notations exist in adjacent fields, notably Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], and BPMN [@bpmnspec] has been profiled for clinical pathways [@braun2014], serverless machine learning [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], human-agent collaboration [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent], organizational modeling [@guerreiro2024], and process simulation [@cimino2025], with mature tooling (bpmn-js [@bpmnjs], bpmn-moddle [@bpmnmoddle]), engines that generate executable code from diagrams [@diagrid], and recent large-language-model authoring aids (ProMoAI [@kourani2024promoai], conversational modeling [@kopke2025]) whose syntactic fluency does not by itself supply domain semantics or validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Dedicated efforts to document and visualize workflows for communication and publication point the same way [@willoughby2017], yet no such profile targets experimental cognitive science.

Across these families the same limitations recur: a representation is machine-facing or human-facing but rarely both; experimental structure stays informal during planning and execution; provenance stops at the computational boundary; and no artifact aligns the scientist, engineer, ethics board, funding agency, and reviewer. No single representation spans the full study lifecycle in a form that all of them can read, validate, and execute (Figure 1).

## 1.3 Desiderata for a study specification language

A specification that closes the process-model gap (§1.1) must meet several desiderata at once.

1. **Single source of truth.** One artifact must serve as the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis pipeline, and the publication figure, so the views cannot drift apart.

2. **Executable rather than merely descriptive.** The specification must run, so that a runner application walks the same file a reviewer reads.

3. **Legible to every audience without code.** Scientists, ethics boards, reviewers, and engineers must read one diagram, not four documents in four formats.

4. **Grounded in standards and gracefully degrading.** The specification must be valid BPMN 2.0 that opens in any compliant tool, with bindings to community data standards such as BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW, and BDM, and its domain extensions must degrade gracefully in a generic BPMN tool such as Camunda.

5. **Process and data on one canvas.** Control flow and typed, schema-bound data must live in the same artifact, joined by data associations.

6. **Extensible without forking.** New domain semantics must plug in as optional layers, so that adding new elements does not change the core.

7. **Agnostic to execution environment.** Who executes the protocol, a person or an artificial agent, must be a runtime choice rather than a property of the diagram, so that one topology enrolls human and computer subjects similarly and the same diagram is sufficient for both.

## 1.4 BPMN as a foundation

Meeting these desiderata is a language design problem. Experimental cognitive science meets the standard criteria for a domain-specific language: recurring structural patterns across studies, expert users who would benefit from a familiar notation rather than general purpose code, and no alternative executable language that already covers the whole experiment lifecycle [@mernik2005dsl]. Rather than invent a new notation, we extend an established one, because a notation researchers, engineers, and reviewers already recognize is a cheaper starting point than a custom one (effective visual notation is itself a research topic [@moody2009physics]).

Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is a mature, ISO-standard graphical language for processes [@white2004introduction]. It already provides what scientific workflows need (events, activities, sub-processes, gateways, data objects, sequence and data flows, and choreography), an established tooling ecosystem (`bpmn-js`, Camunda Modeler, diagrams.net), and a standard serialization, BPMN 2.0 XML, that engineers and analysts recognize and that outlives any single tool.

We build on two of BPMN's extension mechanisms, `extensionElements` and namespaced attributes, which let authors add domain-specific elements inside a new namespace so a BPMN parser ignores them gracefully while a domain-aware tool validates and renders them [@magnani2009bpdmn]. The same mechanism underlies the domain profiles above, catalogued and classified against the BPMN core [@zarour2019; @braun2014classification]; experimental cognitive science is the gap they leave.

<!--
Recent large-language-model-assisted BPMN authoring tools (ProMoAI, BPMN-ChatBot, and related work [@kourani2024promoai; @kourani2024process_modeling_llm]) accelerate diagram authoring from text, but evaluations show that competitive syntactic quality does not translate into domain-specific semantics or domain-specific validation [@lauer2026assessing]. Authoring help is welcome; it is not a substitute for a profile that defines what *cognitive task*, *random assignment*, or *eligibility check* mean inside a process model. That profile is the gap Studyflow fills. -->

The rest of the paper is organized around these desiderata: the framework meets them, the example study exercises them, and the discussion revisits where they hold and where they do not. The framework that follows delivers them as three artifacts: the notation itself (§2.1), the multiple views it projects for different audiences (§2.2), and an open-source reference toolkit that authors and runs it (§2.3).

# 2. The Studyflow framework

A single `.studyflow` file renders in four ways (Study, Gantt, Checklist, Figure) for different audiences, so the same file is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis, and the publication figure. Each desideratum is met by a specific part of the framework (@tbl-requirements).

The seven desiderata of §1.3 and where the framework meets each.

- - Desideratum
  - Where the framework meets it

- - R1 Single source of truth
  - One shared `.studyflow` source is at once the protocol, the runnable study, the analysis, and the figure (§2.1-§2.3)

- - R2 Executable, not merely descriptive
  - The runner walks the same file a reviewer reads (§2.3)

- - R3 Legible to every audience without code
  - Four reader-facing views project from one source (§2.2)

- - R5 Process and data on one canvas
  - Typed, schema-bound data joined to control flow by data associations (§2.1)

- - R6 Extensible without forking
  - A layered, tool-independent LinkML schema (§2.1, §2.3)

- - R7 Executor-agnostic
  - One executor interface behind the runner, demonstrated end to end in §3.2 (§2.3)

## 2.1 Formal definition

A Studyflow is a typed, attributed directed graph, a tuple $(N, E, T, \tau, \lambda)$, where $N$ is a finite set of nodes (events, activities, and gateways), $E \subseteq N \times N$ is a set of directed edges (sequence flows and data associations), $T$ is the set of node types the language defines, $\tau: N \to T$ assigns a type to each node, and $\lambda$ attaches typed attributes to each node, such as the `instrument` of a cognitive task, the `probabilityFunction` of a random gateway, or the `onset` and `duration` that drive the Gantt view. A versioned schema (below) fixes $T$ and the admissible attributes; a diagram is well-formed when its nodes, edges, and attributes validate against it. The graph is general rather than acyclic. Boundary events, message flows, and choreography express the interrupts, loops, and multi-party exchanges experimental procedures contain, which a directed acyclic graph represents only through external control logic. Everything that follows is grounded in this object; the four views are projections of it.

**A standard host notation.** Studyflow realizes this object as a domain-specific profile of BPMN 2.0 [@white2004introduction], tailored to experimental cognitive science. The diagrams stay valid BPMN 2.0 XML and open in any compliant tool (Camunda Modeler, bpmn.io, diagrams.net), and BPMN's extension mechanism (`extensionElements`, namespaced attributes) adds the domain semantics of $T$ and $\lambda$ without breaking the base standard [@stroppi2011; @magnani2009bpdmn].

**What Studyflow inherits.** Studyflow reuses BPMN's full vocabulary for control flow and structure: events (start, end, boundary, timer, error), activities (tasks, sub-processes, call activities), the five gateway types, sequence and message flows, data objects and stores with their associations, pools and lanes, and choreography for multi-agent interactions. These elements keep standard BPMN shapes and behave as the OMG specifies.

**What Studyflow adds.** Four areas extend BPMN with vocabulary experimental research routinely needs. First, a top-level **study container** groups every other element and carries study-level metadata (title, version, authors, runtime). Second, **domain-specific activity types** specialize the generic BPMN task with research-meaningful kinds (cognitive tasks, questionnaires, instructions, rest periods, video games, and a curated cognitive battery); each shows a distinctive icon but remains a normal BPMN task underneath. Third, **research-specific data elements** add bindings to community schemas (BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], CSVW) and our own Behaverse Data Model (BDM) [@bdm] on top of BPMN's generic data objects. A small **data-operations vocabulary** (map, filter, reduce, group, transform, compose) marks the *kind* of transformation on a task, so data flow is visible at a glance. Fourth, **research gateways** encode branching patterns specific to experimental design: a random gateway for randomization, a stratified-allocation gateway, and an eligibility gateway that lists inclusion and exclusion criteria. Optional temporal attributes (onset, duration, progress) attach to activities and events, so the Gantt view derives trial schedules and visit calendars from the same diagram.

**What Studyflow deliberately leaves alone.** Studyflow leaves BPMN's serialization conventions, XML namespaces, element identifiers, and base shapes untouched; the domain extensions live inside BPMN's native extension slot, so a generic renderer ignores them gracefully while a Studyflow-aware tool validates and renders them.

**A layered set of schemas.** The vocabulary is split into a small core and optional domain extensions that load on demand (Figure 2). The core covers the language scaffolding and a companion cognitive layer, while four optional layers cover specific domains: a cognitive-assessment battery, generic process orchestration, large-scale data transformation, and multimodal acquisition for EEG and eye tracking. New domains plug in by writing a schema, without changing the core. Supplementary Table S1 has the complete catalog; @tbl-elements gives a representative subset.

**A machine-readable specification.** The language is defined by a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml], the single source of truth for element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules, mirrored by the runtime YAML schemas the BPMN tooling reads. Listing 1 gives the schema for the study container and a cognitive task: a `CognitiveTask` specializes a generic data-operation activity, requires an `instrument`, and carries an inline `configurations` block. Listing 2 shows how a research gateway maps onto BPMN. A `RandomGateway` and an `EligibilityGateway` both specialize a standard `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway`, so they serialize and render as ordinary BPMN gateways while carrying the attributes that make randomization and eligibility explicit. A diagram that uses them stays valid BPMN 2.0 and degrades gracefully. The on-disk XML appears where the worked example encodes its n-back task (Listing 3).

**Listing 1.** Studyflow language specification (LinkML excerpt; descriptions abridged). The schema fixes element types, required attributes, and validation rules independently of any tool.

```yaml
Study:
  class_uri: bpmn:Process
  tree_root: true
  attributes:
    name:
      range: string
      required: true
    version:
      range: string
    authors:
      range: string
      multivalued: true
    runtime:
      range: RuntimeEnum

CognitiveTask:
  is_a: DataOperationActivity        # a specialized BPMN activity
  class_uri: cognitive:CognitiveTask
  attributes:
    instrument:                      # psychopy, jspsych, labjs, ...
      range: string
      required: true
    configurations:                  # instrument-specific, inline YAML
      range: YAMLString
```

**Listing 2.** Two research gateways, each a specialization of `bpmn:ExclusiveGateway` (runtime schema excerpt; abridged). The diagram stays valid BPMN while the extension carries the randomization and eligibility semantics.

```yaml
- name: RandomGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: algorithm
      type: AssignmentAlgorithmEnum
      default: probabilistic
    - name: probabilityFunction
      type: String
      default: uniform
- name: EligibilityGateway
  superClass:
    - bpmn:ExclusiveGateway
    - bpmn:BaseElement
  properties:
    - name: inclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
    - name: exclusionCriteria
      type: MarkdownString
      isMany: true
```

## 2.2 Multiple views: Study / Gantt / Checklist / Figure

Each view is a projection $\pi_{\text{view}}$ over the formal object: it keeps the nodes, edges, and attributes a given audience needs and drops the rest. The Gantt view, for instance, keeps the nodes whose $\lambda$ carries an `onset` or `duration` and lays them on a time axis, while the Study view sets those temporal attributes aside. A single `.studyflow` source therefore renders in four ways, each suited to a different stakeholder (Figure 5), and all four read the same file, so changes propagate automatically.

**Study view.** The default rendering is a BPMN-like graph that shows every element and connection. It is *structural*, showing what happens and in what order without committing to wall-clock timing, and it serves Methods sections, reviewers checking logical structure, and pipeline authors wiring up data flow.

**Gantt view.** A Gantt-style rendering places time-sensitive elements along a time axis. BPMN has timer events but no native way to express activity duration, scheduled onset, or progress, so Studyflow attaches these as optional attributes on activities and events: **onset**, **duration**, and **progress** (percentage or label). Resource allocation uses BPMN pools and lanes directly to group rows, with no separate attribute. When the temporal attributes are present the view renders automatically, and the same mechanism scales from trial-level timing (stimulus duration, ITI, response window) to study-level timing (visit schedule, follow-ups), with milestones as zero-duration elements and hierarchical Gantts mapping onto sub-processes. It suits longitudinal studies and SPIRIT-style schedules of enrolment and assessment [@spirit2013].

**Checklist view.** This task-oriented view flattens the diagram into a list of activities with their items and status, drawn from an optional `checklist` attribute (a markdown list) on every element. It supports two uses: *running studies day-to-day* (what is next, what is done) and *adhering to reporting guidelines* (CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, PRISMA, and CARE), where guideline items map to the elements that satisfy them, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. Checklists ship inside the `.studyflow` file and export to JSON or Markdown for external task managers.

**Figure view.** The Figure view renders a diagram as a publication-ready SVG in which per-element annotations decide what is shown or hidden. A manuscript figure usually needs a curated subset of the full diagram, the protocol without the data layer or a single highlighted path through a branch, so rather than redraw by hand, an author marks elements to show or hide and exports the curated SVG. The exported SVG embeds the complete `.studyflow` source as metadata, so the published figure is the runnable file itself rather than a picture of the study: a reader can lift the source back out, open it in the modeler, and re-run it. Because the visibility annotations live in the same `extensionElements` slot as the rest of the vocabulary, the figure stays valid BPMN and tied to the study it depicts. This is the mechanism behind the published CONSORT figure.

::: {.list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l" tbl-colwidths="[65,35]"}
- - If you need to communicate...
  - Use

- - Procedural structure, branching, data flow
  - Study view

- - Wall-clock timing, schedules, durations
  - Gantt view

- - Coverage against a reporting checklist or protocol
  - Checklist view

- - A publication figure with selected elements shown or hidden
  - Figure view
:::

## 2.3 The Studyflow toolkit: a modeler and a runner

Two open-source applications (MIT-licensed, client-side, browser-only, with no server dependency) sit on top of the language: a modeler that authors diagrams and a runner that executes them. They are fully working prototypes rather than production software: reference implementations whose purpose is to show that the specification is authorable, executable, and machine-readable. Both are clients of the specification rather than owners of it. The language stays a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] independent of either application, so third-party tools (linters, converters, and execution engines) can target the same specification, and each component, the schema, the modeler, the runner, and the data server that hosts published studies, evolves on its own while one `.studyflow` source ties them together.

**The modeler** authors, inspects, simulates, validates, and publishes diagrams (Figure 3), and its interface is *schema-driven*: the palette, the inspector, and the validation rules are generated from the layered moddle schemas, so adding an element type or attribute updates the interface automatically. A simulation mode steps through the diagram and runs the gateway logic, catching dead branches and missing conditions before a study runs. Export to PNG and SVG produces publication-ready figures whose SVGs embed the source XML, so the exported figure is the runnable file. Publishing uploads the diagram to our data server [@bds], which builds its own participant-facing interface from the diagram structure; each publish creates a new server-side version, so studies already in the field keep working when authors push updates.

**The runner** walks a participant or an artificial agent through a diagram node by node, reached from the modeler's *Run* button, a URL parameter, or a file upload. It validates the diagram, traverses it from start to end rendering each node as a step, and applies any completion code or redirect at the end; an optional random seed makes branching deterministic. It ships the step kinds the worked example needs (consent, instruction, questionnaire, cognitive task, and a generic fallback) and accepts new ones as self-registering folders, so a domain group can add a custom step without forking it. Its central design, one message-passing executor interface behind which human and agent actors stand, drives the worked example of §3.2 and is detailed in §5.4. The runner is above all a proof of concept that one `.studyflow` file is machine-readable and spans the use cases the language targets, so its current gaps are engineering scope rather than expressiveness.

Figure 4 walks a participant from consent through an instruction, a questionnaire, and a cognitive task to the end screen, all on the same diagram authored above [FILL: runner screenshots from the seed-42 walkthrough].

# 3. A complete study, from protocol to publication

This section exercises the framework's claims, showing that desiderata R1-R7 hold when a real study is run, not only described. We follow one registered human-and-agent agreement trial that stresses every part of the framework in one file: ten people and a cohort of artificial agents perform the same six-task battery, allocated to a self-paced and a time-pressured path. It is a demonstration, not a finding about agents; the agent-cohort table (@tbl-agents) and figures carry [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs] and show the shape of the result, not the result itself.

The same `.studyflow` file is the only input at every stage, design, enrollment, analysis, modeling, and reporting, so each stage reads or extends the artifact the stage before it left.

## 3.1 Design: a registered human/agent agreement

Our worked example asks an agreement question: across the six constructs the battery probes, do people and agents reach approximate agreement, and where do they diverge? We design it as a registered randomized controlled trial so the comparison is trustworthy before it runs. Each subject is allocated to one of two paths, self-paced and time-pressured, with task order counterbalanced within each, so the paths test whether agreement is robust under a timing manipulation. The protocol carries the scaffolding a registered study needs: consent, eligibility screening, seed-controlled random allocation to the two paths, and the structure a journal will later expect.

In current practice this scaffolding is spread across a registry entry, an ethics PDF, a recruitment system, and a CONSORT flow diagram drawn at write-up time, none of them a machine-readable view of the others [@moher2012; @rennie2001; @hopewell2025consort]. The flow diagram, in particular, is a participant-tracking schematic; its four standard rows are enrollment, allocation, follow-up, and analysis, and attrition counts annotate each transition. It is a *document* about the trial rather than the *spec* that drove it. Studyflow makes the document and the spec one file.

We start from the CONSORT 2025 reference diagram that ships with the modeler; authors can fork it, parameterize it, and run it as the actual protocol of a new trial [@hopewell2025consort]. Figure 6 compares three artifacts: (a) the standard CONSORT 2025 reference flow as published by the CONSORT group, (b) a Studyflow reproduction encoded with the same labels and pathways, and (c) an annotated comparison whose left path uses Studyflow boundary error events and whose right path uses the traditional text-and-box treatment.

The key mechanical difference is how attrition is represented. In the traditional figure, each "Excluded / Did not receive / Lost to follow-up / Discontinued" box is an unconnected annotation that sits next to the column of follow-up activities, and readers must infer that these counts subtract from the main flow. In the Studyflow diagram, attrition is encoded as a *boundary error event* attached to the activity that participants left from. Exclusion at screening hangs off the eligibility gateway, non-receipt of intervention off the two allocation tasks, loss to follow-up and discontinuation off the follow-up tasks, and exclusion from analysis off the analysis tasks. Each event ends in an error end event with a labeled count. This has three consequences. First, the diagram's topology now matches the trial's topology, so a participant lost during follow-up exits along an edge that starts at the follow-up activity itself, rather than an arrow drawn from a side annotation. Second, summing attrition becomes a graph operation instead of a manual exercise, so a Studyflow-aware validator can check that no row's outbound counts exceed its inbound count. Third, the boundary error event is the same primitive that BPMN uses to model interrupts in any business process, so the diagram stays valid BPMN 2.0 and inherits the standard execution semantics for error handling [@stroppi2011; @ait2024bpmn_humanagent].

In the file, each attrition path is a few lines of standard BPMN: a boundary error event attached to the activity that participants leave from, wired to an error end event that carries the count.

```xml
<bpmn2:boundaryEvent id="Dropout" name="Dropped out (n=...)"
                     attachedToRef="Battery">
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_Dropout_Excluded</bpmn2:outgoing>
  <bpmn2:errorEventDefinition id="ErrorDef_Dropout" />
</bpmn2:boundaryEvent>
```

The diagram carries domain semantics alongside the BPMN structure. The enrollment start event references a participant-facing consent PDF, so a runner reaching this node renders the consent screen before any randomization. The screening task carries a markdown checklist (demographic intake, medical history, baseline cognitive screen) that drives the Checklist view; the eligibility and randomization gateways are typed as such; each battery task declares itself a cognitive task with its own inline parameter block (for the n-back: the N level, stimulus duration, inter-trial interval, and trials per block); and the allocation, follow-up, and analysis tasks carry checklists describing protocol obligations. A single file therefore serves four readers at once: the trial registry (a registered protocol with explicit randomization and eligibility criteria), the ethics board (consent content and per-task checklists), the data-collection platform (the embedded cognitive-task instrument and its parameters), and the journal (the CONSORT figure with attrition flows already wired). The mechanism is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011]: each reader interprets the layer it cares about. The union of those layers, rendered together, *is* a CONSORT diagram.

Where CONSORT structures the *report*, SPIRIT structures the *plan*. The same study also renders as a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, based on a worked SPIRIT template that the modeler ships. Its 34 checklist items across 9 topics map onto the Gantt view [@chan2025spirit; @spirit2013]. A SPIRIT plan and a CONSORT report are then the same file at two points in its lifecycle: the schedule before randomization, and the flow diagram with attrition counts written into the labels of the boundary error events once the study has run.

Because the executor is a runtime parameter, the same flow enrolls, allocates, follows up, and analyzes an agent exactly where it does a person. CONSORT and SPIRIT originate in human trials, and reading agents as co-subjects in one flow is a deliberate extension the unified representation makes natural: a run that crashes or falls out of set leaves the trial along the same edge a participant lost to follow-up does.

## 3.2 Enroll and run: one diagram runs the trial for every subject

This stage runs both kinds of co-subject through one diagram, making Studyflow's central idea concrete: *who executes the protocol is a runtime decision, not a property of the diagram*. Participants and agents traverse the identical enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology and write into one schema-conformant table.

**The battery.** Our study administers a six-task Behaverse battery spanning working memory (n-back and digit span), attention (multiple-object tracking), processing speed (pattern comparison), fluid reasoning (matrix reasoning), and set-shifting (card sorting). These six constructs are the space across which people and agents are compared, and one `.studyflow` source drives every task and actor. The n-back serves as the worked example below, a near-universal probe of working memory [@owen2005nback], and the other five use the same machinery.

**The round-trip: enroll, allocate, and follow up.** We built the battery in the modeler as one diagram that orchestrates the four CONSORT stages for both paths: enrollment through consent and baseline questionnaires, an eligibility gateway, randomized allocation to the self-paced and time-pressured paths, and follow-up through the six tasks, with task order counterbalanced within each path. Each task is itself a nested timeline of blocks (a warm-up, the test blocks, and any adaptive staircase) that prose and slides flatten but the diagram keeps explicit. Loaded into the runner, the diagram is checked for required parameters and then walked one node at a time (Figure 4). The same seed-controlled random gateway allocates every subject, so a URL parameter (`?seed=42`) fixes the path assignment, the within-task stimulus order, and every random branch, and the protocol a participant or an agent encounters is identical across runs at a given seed. Responses are a separate matter: human and language-model responses are sampled rather than seeded, so we record the seed with the model identity and version and report agent results as run-level aggregates rather than a single canonical trace.

**Encoding the trials.** Figure 7 places the traditional slide-style n-back figure next to the Studyflow equivalent. The slide is intuitive but underspecified: timing values often live only in the caption, the trial-block boundary stays implicit, and decisions like "what counts as a correct match" are buried in the analysis code. Studyflow instead encodes the trial as an explicit subgraph: a stimulus activity, a boundary timer for the response window, a second for the inter-trial interval, and annotations labeling the target and non-target branches. The trial-by-trial encoding in Figure 7 is illustrative; for runs beyond a handful of trials the same logic compresses into a single cognitive task whose inline configuration declares the N level, stream, trial count, stimulus duration, and inter-trial interval, which the runner expands into individual trials (Listing 3). The same compression applies to every task in the battery. Each trial is logged to our trials schema (BDM [@bdm], Psych-DS-compatible [@psychds]), so the same diagram produces a CSV whose columns the schema fixes and whose meaning the diagram fixes, identically across all six tasks; a third party with only those two files can reconstruct what each row means without the modeler.

**Listing 3.** The n-back task serialized in a `.studyflow` file (BPMN 2.0 XML, abridged). The task is a standard `bpmn:task` carrying a `cognitive:task` extension; its inline `cognitive:configurations` block declares the N level, the stimulus stream, and the timing, which the runner expands into individual trials.

```xml
<bpmn2:task id="Task_NB" name="N-back (text)">
  <bpmn2:extensionElements>
    <cognitive:task scene="NB" configMode="inline">
      <cognitive:configurations>
        NValue: 2
        Feature: Letters
        Streams:
          - StimulusValue: [3, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3, 1]
        StreamSize: 12
        StimulusDisplayDuration: 0.5
        InterStimulusInterval: 1.5
      </cognitive:configurations>
    </cognitive:task>
  </bpmn2:extensionElements>
  <bpmn2:incoming>Flow_B_Start_NB</bpmn2:incoming>
  <bpmn2:outgoing>Flow_NB_DS</bpmn2:outgoing>
</bpmn2:task>
```

**One executor, many actors.** The runner administers every actor through one message-passing executor interface (Figure 8; the actor-model design and signature are in §5.4). Per trial it sends the stimulus, the allowed responses, the timing constraint, and where needed a rendered frame, and records the response and, where applicable, the response time under the common schema. Each actor keeps its own state behind that interface, a participant's session, an agent's policy, a recurrent hidden state, or a language model's context, so the runner never reaches inside it; human and agent co-subjects are actors in one shared space. Each realizes an Actor element the language types by `actorType` (human, LLM, agent, or instrument; §2.1), and this study fills the executor with four: a human, a reinforcement-learning agent, a recurrent model, and a language model, the last two both carrying the agent type. The *human* actor renders each trial in a participant-facing interface and blocks until a person responds; ten participants ran the battery this way. *Reinforcement-learning agents* run through CogEnv [@ansarinia2022cogenv], which drives RL policies through the bot interface the Behaverse assessment application exposes, so an agent meets the same stimuli, response options, and time constraints a participant does; a random or scripted policy also validates the protocol, surfacing stuck states and timing edge cases before any human sits down. *Recurrent cognitive models* run through CogPonder [@ansarinia2023cogponder], our differentiable PonderNet-based model that reproduces human accuracy and response times by controlling how long it ponders before committing; it returns both a response and a pondered response time, so the cohort gains a process model whose latencies are predicted from the task, not sampled from a prompt. *Language-model agents* run through a package that sends each trial to the configured model with a free-form prompt steering a simulated participant (trait, target accuracy, mistake rate); vision-capable models also read the rendered frame, so the battery's spatial tasks (object tracking, matrix reasoning, card sorting), which carry no useful textual stimulus, stay tractable. If an actor replies outside the allowed set, the runner records the mismatch and falls back to a uniform random choice, so a transient failure cannot silently corrupt the dataset.

Instantiating an executor package is the agent's enrollment record, with model identity and version pinned to every run; the out-of-set fallback is the attrition mechanism, so a run that times out or crashes exits along a boundary error event and is counted as a dropout in the same CONSORT flow.

**The agent cohort: a matrix enrolled across the objective space.** We enroll a matrix of agents across the whole battery, rather than scoring one agent on one task, so the agents meet the same six constructs the people traverse. We cross three factors. The first is *model*: a uniform-random baseline, a recurrent cognitive model (CogPonder), a reinforcement-learning policy through CogEnv, several open-weight text models served locally through Ollama, and a commercial vision-language model (Claude). The second is *trait*: response profiles from prior characterizations of participants, a careful high-accuracy responder with the conservative decision criterion the diffusion model formalizes [@ratcliff2008diffusion], a fatigued responder marked by intermittent attentional lapses [@robertson1997oops], and a speed-accuracy-tradeoff responder at the fast, error-prone end of that classic trade [@wickelgren1977sat]. The third is *task*: the six battery tasks. A trait is fixed by a free-form prompt held constant across the battery while each task supplies its own response instructions, so each model produces a profile across constructs rather than a single score; for the prompt-free families the same axis is set natively, through the pondering cost in the recurrent model and the policy in the reinforcement-learning agent. We administered every model-by-trait-by-task cell at seed 42, fixing the stimulus order and sampling the responses. @tbl-agents reports accuracy, median response time, and the out-of-set fallback rate for every cell [FILL: values from the seed-42 runs], and Figure 9 shows the accuracy and response-time profiles across tasks [FILL: rendered from the same runs]; the random baseline sits near chance, and the open-weight models run the same battery without an external API [FILL: the observed open- versus closed-weight pattern]. This is the "few models, many items" regime [@ansarinia2022cogenv] extended across tasks: rather than rank many models on a single task, we vary the diagram (task, difficulty, response window, trait) and profile a cohort of agents over a whole battery of parametrically related items.

::: {#tbl-agents .list-table header-rows=1 aligns="l,l,l,r,r,r" tbl-colwidths="[16,16,16,16,18,18]"}

- - Model
  - Trait
  - Task
  - Accuracy
  - Median RT (ms)
  - Fallback rate

- - [FILL]

**Beyond one participant.** The same notation scales in two directions the diagram already expresses, both runner roadmap items (§4.5). When the *interaction itself* is the unit, BPMN 2.0's **choreography task** models a directed exchange with an explicit initiator [@pufahl2022; @decker2011choreography]; a choreography task between a human and an LLM agent is the same primitive as one between two humans, and the diagram validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema even though the runner does not yet traverse it [@stroppi2011]. When the subject is artificial, the case for a machine-readable procedural specification only grows as discovery moves toward multi-agent laboratories [@ghareeb2025], and alignment research makes it from the measurement side, comparing agents and humans across a space of objectives [@nayebi2026alignment].

Read off that shared table, the cohort of agents and the ten people form one comparison across the six constructs, so where they agree and where they diverge is a property of a single artifact.

## 3.3 Measure agreement: human-agent comparison and the CONSORT flow

Because both kinds of subject wrote to one schema-bound table, this stage reads the agreement question off that table and closes the CONSORT flow by counting the analysis exclusions on the same record. The analysis that produces this read-out is usually a script, an R or Python notebook whose structure (the order of operations, their dependencies, the kind of each step) lives in code and comments rather than in a machine-readable record. Studyflow's data operations give every operation an explicit type (map, filter, group, reduce, expand, transform, compose), so the *kind* of work each step does is visible in the diagram; with dataset, store, and schema elements, the diagram becomes a complete, machine-readable pre-registration of the analysis.

We analyze the trials through a typed pipeline: read the raw trials; filter invalid ones (RT < 100 ms, missing data, fallback-flagged rows), the analysis-exclusion row of the CONSORT flow, applying one rule set to both populations so a failed human trial and an out-of-set agent run are removed at the same node and counted together; map to derived measures; branch at an exclusive gateway on the comparison of interest; group by task, actor, and trait; reduce to per-group accuracy, median RT, and standard errors; route through a manual review of outliers; and render and write the summary table and figures, each to a schema-declared dataset. Three properties are not optional: the conditional branch is visible in the topology rather than buried inside an `if`; the manual review has an explicit place in the diagram, making it harder to skip; and the schema on the output table is part of the spec rather than implicit in the column names.

Because the same diagram carries process and typed data together, the human-and-agent agreement is auditable from one artifact rather than asserted across mismatched ones. Activities sit on the sequence-flow graph, while datasets, stores, catalogs, schemas, and snapshots sit on a parallel data-flow graph that BPMN data associations, drawn as dashed edges, connect. Every dataset declares its format (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, or generic) and a schema, inline or external; tabular data carries a CSVW body or a schema reference [@hoytO3GuidelinesOpen2024; @csvw], while non-tabular data documents tensor dimensions, dtypes, and units. Bindings to BIDS [@bids], Psych-DS [@psychds], and BDM [@bdm] are typed contracts that the modeler validates and the runner respects, so an analyst can confirm from the diagram alone that a downstream task consumes exactly the column an upstream task produced.

Concretely, Figure 10 shows the RT-analysis subprocess beside the equivalent dplyr code. The diagram encodes the same chained pipeline a tidyverse user would write as `filter |> mutate |> group_by |> summarize`, but it adds two commitments. First, the inputs and outputs are typed (BDM trials level in, models level out), registered in a catalog, and physically stored in a backing store (a DuckDB-plus-Parquet ducklake in our example). Second, the analysis task's composed-operation marker declares which primitive operations the task may perform, so tooling can reject any implementation that touches an undeclared column or runs an unauthorized operation.

Pre-registration of analysis then becomes the diagram itself. In current practice a pre-registered plan is free text on a registry website, with no machine-checkable link to the code that is eventually run; under the Studyflow encoding the diagram is the spec and the dplyr pipeline is one valid implementation, and any divergence between the two shows up in the data-operation markers and the input and output schemas. The modeler reduces visual density with collapsible layers, turning the data layer off for the high-level protocol and on for the full dependency graph; whether this makes large process-plus-data diagrams more legible than the artifacts they replace is an unvalidated claim.

The worked dataset is the seed-42 agent cohort and the ten-participant human battery, both written to the same trials schema [FILL: summary RT values and per-construct agreement once the analysis is run].

## 3.4 Model agreement: a human-versus-agent classifier

The analysis stage reads agreement off group summaries, and the same trials can feed a model that learns the read-out: a classifier of human versus agent that locates where the two populations separate, a model of the response-time distribution across tasks and difficulty, or, with neural recordings, a multimodal predictor. Because both cohorts wrote one schema-bound table, such a classifier trains on the same rows the comparison reads and is authored in the same diagram rather than a separate codebase. ML pipelines suffer the same fragmentation as experimental protocols, with the model card, feature engineering, training script, deployment config, and retraining triggers scattered across repositories and cron jobs; Studyflow's data operations, gateways, and schema-bound data elements apply to them as cleanly as to behavioral analyses, so an analysis and a training pipeline share one notation with different operators [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml].

Beyond the classifier, the same notation expresses a full multimodal preprocessing and training pipeline that harmonizes EEG, fMRI, and behavioral recordings across heterogeneous public datasets, which we specify in Figure 11 rather than run here. It makes three properties explicit that prose hides: provenance is the diagram, since every derived artifact traces back to its raw source through the nodes that produced it; the multiverse is first-class, with defensible analytical paths as explicit branches rather than version-controlled forks [@steegen2016multiverse]; and cross-dataset interoperability is a schema decision, so a preprocessing subprocess defined once applies to every dataset in the same format. Behavioral data is converted to BDM trials [@defossez2020bdm], and the same encoding extends to containerized HPC execution and to downstream training, fine-tuning, evaluation, monitoring, and data-governance subprocesses [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml; @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health].

## 3.5 Report: the file that ran the trial is the CONSORT figure and the benchmark

The lifecycle closes where it began, with the reporting guidelines that shaped the design. Because the trial ran inside the same file, the CONSORT figure is not redrawn at write-up time; the modeler's Figure view exports it from the protocol that enrolled, allocated, followed up, and analyzed both cohorts, with the attrition counts already written into the boundary error events and the `.studyflow` source embedded in the SVG as metadata. The figure that appears in the paper is, literally, the file that ran the trial, so the one exported source is at once the CONSORT report and the specification of the agreement benchmark it ran.

Reporting against a guideline then becomes a property the diagram can be checked for, rather than a PDF assembled alongside it. Each guideline is, in structure, a controlled vocabulary, a checklist, and sometimes a flow diagram, and Studyflow handles all of them the same way: checklist items become entries in the optional `checklist` attribute, flow diagrams become Studyflow renderings with boundary error events for attrition, and vocabulary becomes labels on activities, gateways, and data elements. Because the checklist attribute is machine-readable, the Checklist view shows the items as a markdown list, each linked back to the element that satisfies it, so a study can be audited without leaving the diagram. The EQUATOR network catalogs these standards [@simera2010equator]; @tbl-guidelines lists the eleven most widely used, with Studyflow's current coverage. The two that ship today (CONSORT and SPIRIT) exercise the full mechanism; the entries marked Roadmap are authoring work rather than missing capability, since the elements, attributes, and Checklist view they need are already in place and each takes about half a day to template.

Two guidelines ship as worked templates today: CONSORT 2025, whose 30-item checklist [@hopewell2025consort] maps onto the shipped template, and SPIRIT 2025, whose 34 items across 9 topics [@chan2025spirit] map onto a Gantt view (Figure 12) that serves as both schedule and checklist. The pattern recurs across the catalog, with STROBE and PRISMA next: PRISMA 2020 [@page2021prisma] standardized the study-flow diagrams that are visual instances of what Studyflow generalizes, TIDieR [@hoffmann2014tidier] makes intervention details first-class items that map onto the participant branch, and ARRIVE 2.0 [@percie2020arrive], with its history of endorsement without adherence, supplies the animal-research counterpart.

Reporting guidelines and execution specifications need not be different artifacts. At publication, the manuscript ships three artifacts that are all views of one source: the exported figure that is at once the CONSORT report and the benchmark specification, the Checklist-view audit against the target guideline, and the `.studyflow` file itself, paired with the schema-conformant trials table that holds both subject populations. From these, a reader can reconstruct what every element and every column means, and read where the people and the agents agree across the battery and where they diverge, without rerunning the trial.

---

# 4. Discussion

## 4.1 What Studyflow changes: from divergent artifacts to one auditable diagram

Current practice keeps the *protocol*, the *code*, and the *figure* as three separate artifacts. They begin in agreement and drift apart over a project's life. Studyflow consolidates them into one source-of-truth file. The same CONSORT diagram is the participant flow figure, the spec a reviewer audits, and the artifact the data-collection applications step through. The file is at once the protocol text, the experiment loop, and the executable tasks. The response time pipeline above is both the analysis section and the transformation script. Because there is only one source, these views can no longer drift apart. That source is plain XML (or similar serializations such as YAML or JSON), so it diffs in Git and embeds in image metadata, bringing procedural specifications under the version control discipline that already governs data and code; its specification is a standalone schema; and reporting guideline conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked for.

One protocol, many actors, so a human-and-agent agreement trial becomes one auditable artifact. The same source runs human participants and artificial agents as actors behind one execution interface; the worked example uses this to author a registered trial in which people and a cohort of artificial agents are co-subjects in one study. The example is one practical pathway human-AI alignment research calls for, comparing a set of agents, humans included, across a space of objectives [@nayebi2026alignment; @nayebi2025corrigible]. The claim stays at the level of notation: Studyflow can author such a benchmark, and its objective space is limited to six cognitive tasks. A benchmark for AI systems no longer needs to be written three times in three formats; the protocol stays one artifact.

One property underlies them all: reproducibility becomes a feature of the shared artifact, not of documentation kept beside it. The diagram an ethics board approves is the diagram participants and agents run and the diagram the figures come from, so the human-and-agent comparison is auditable from one source.

## 4.2 Relationship to existing ecosystems

Studyflow sits at the intersection of four ecosystems, and it does not aim to replace any of them.

**Workflow engines.** A family of engines solves a problem Studyflow leaves alone: scalable, reproducible execution on heterogeneous compute, among them Nextflow, the Common Workflow Language (CWL), the Workflow Description Language (WDL), Pegasus, Apache Airflow, Kedro, NiPype, and Pydra [@zhao2008scientific_workflows; @cuevasvicenttin2013workflows; @nextflow; @cwl; @pydra]. Their representations target machines and developers rather than domain experts, and they model a workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which fits data pipelines with fixed inputs and outputs. Much of scientific inquiry is iterative, however, and BPMN expresses loops directly through sequence flows, boundary events, and choreography [@ghareeb2025], whereas a DAG emulates them through external control logic. The two are complementary: Studyflow sits *above* such systems, since a task can reference an external script (a Nextflow process, a Kedro node, a NiPype workflow) and a downstream tool can compile the protocol diagram into an executable graph [e.g., @ghosh2025reproducible_digital_health]. By the same logic, Studyflow leaves process mining to other tools, which can consume its traces directly [@vanderaalst2016process].

**Data standards.** BIDS, BDM, Psych-DS, and CSVW prescribe how datasets are structured but say nothing about the process that produced them [@bids; @bdm; @psychds; @csvw]. Studyflow describes that process and references these standards through dataset, table, and schema elements: a BIDS-typed dataset linked to a "Record EEG" task tells both *what* was collected and *how*.

**Reporting guidelines.** CONSORT, SPIRIT, STROBE, and STARD, with their siblings, enforce structure at the publication stage [@moher2012; @spirit2013; @strobe; @stard], and today conformance is checked manually against PDF supplements. Authored as Studyflow, a guideline carries its checklist items as elements, so conformance becomes a property the diagram can be checked for rather than a separate checklist.

**Other BPMN profiles.** BPMN4CP for clinical pathways [@braun2014], BPMN4sML for serverless ML [@tetzlaff2022bpmn4sml], and the human-agent extension [@ait2024bpmn_humanagent] are sibling profiles in adjacent domains, and Studyflow's architecture follows the same pattern. Visual modeling languages already used in life sciences, such as Systems Biology Graphical Notation [@novere2009], confirm both the appetite for graphical formalization and the importance of domain-specific vocabulary [@norouzi2025semantic_processes].

Just as Studyflow does not aim to replace these ecosystems, it does not aim to be an ontology of experimental design. Process ontologies are numerous, but they tend to have high upfront cost and low reuse [@norouzi2025semantic_processes], so we have aimed for a profile small enough to learn from one example and a glossary, enforced by tooling rather than by careful inspection.

A shared architectural pattern across several adjacent systems makes Studyflow's position concrete. LinkML [@moxon2025linkml], NIDM Results [@maumet2016nidm], BIDS [@bids], and ARTEM-IS [@styles2021artemis; @soskic2025artemis] share one pattern but occupy *different planes*. The pattern has a schema layer, a human-friendly authoring layer, and one or more machine-readable outputs, and each system covers a different aspect of a study: LinkML over the data model, NIDM-Results over analysis outputs, BIDS over multimodal data organization, and ARTEM-IS over methods reporting. The procedural plane of this pattern, a machine-readable, human-authorable specification of the study *process*, is the gap that Studyflow fills. ARTEM-IS is the closest existing precedent in spirit: it commits the EEG methods reporting community to structured templates that emit both human-readable forms and JSON. Studyflow generalizes the same commitment, from EEG methods reporting to whole procedural specification.

## 4.3 Objections and alternate views

A profile that spans protocol, execution, analysis, and publication invites objections from both audiences, and we take the strongest ones in turn rather than wait for them at review. Each is stated as a skeptic would state it, and each answer concedes what is true before saying what is left standing.

**"BPMN is heavyweight, and this is one more notation to learn."** This is a fair cost, and we do not claim it away. A reader new to flowcharts still faces a learning curve, gentler than a custom language would impose, because BPMN's visual grammar is already recognized across engineering and analysis [@white2004introduction; @moody2009physics]. We also keep the surface small: the always-loaded layers are the language core and a companion cognitive layer, and everything else is an optional domain layer a study never has to open (Table S1). The bet is that one worked example and a glossary are enough to start, and a usability study is the proper test of it.

**"This is just a flowchart with extra labels."** A box-and-arrow figure communicates at a glance, and Studyflow keeps that affordance. The difference is that the same artifact is executable rather than only descriptive (R2): a runner walks the file a reviewer reads, stable identifiers let it diff in Git and embed in an SVG export (R1), and the elements validate against a versioned LinkML schema, so *cognitive task*, *random gateway*, and *eligibility check* carry checkable meaning rather than informal labels [@moxon2025linkml]. A flowchart that an ethics board reads, a participant runs, and a figure exports from one source is doing more than a flowchart.

**"Reading artificial agents as co-subjects in a CONSORT trial overclaims; CONSORT is for human trials."** We agree that CONSORT was written for human randomized trials, and we do not assert that an agent cohort inherits the ethical or inferential standing of a human cohort. The claim stays at the level of notation: the enroll, allocate, run, and analyze topology is one shape, and because the executor is a runtime decision (R7), the same shape can route a human cohort and an agent cohort into one schema-conformant table. The six constructs are the objective space of that read, not safety values, and the alignment account supplies the framing, not a proof that the agents are subjects in the human sense [@nayebi2026alignment; @nayebi2025corrigible]. What we demonstrate is that Studyflow can author such a benchmark; the standing of the agent cohort remains a question for the alignment and ethics literatures.

**"A single source of truth is brittle and risks tool lock-in."** A single source does concentrate risk, and the design answers that directly. The specification is a LinkML schema maintained separately from the modeler, so third-party linters, converters, and renderers can target it without depending on any single application (R6), and the artifact on disk is plain BPMN 2.0 XML that opens in any compliant tool and degrades gracefully when a tool does not know the domain extensions (R4) [@white2004introduction; @magnani2009bpdmn]. The modeler is one open-source client of that schema, so a project that abandons our tooling keeps a valid, tool-independent file. We treat the concentration as the feature and the tool-independence as the safeguard.

## 4.4 Limitations

The scope limits of the current system fall into two kinds, and we keep them apart because conflating them would misstate what the language can express. The first kind is a choice of scope in the *tooling*, where the diagram is fully expressive at modeling time and each gap corresponds to a roadmap item. The Studyflow Runner ships a fixed set of step kinds, does not support parallel gateways, falls back to a uniform pick where balanced stratified allocation is called for, and does not yet traverse choreography tasks, although the diagram that declares them validates against the BPMN 2.0 choreography schema [@stroppi2011]. The multi-actor setup likewise works today for the Behaverse battery, the 22 tasks recognized by our data server, CogEnv, CogPonder, and the runner; a custom PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] or jsPsych task referenced from a diagram still runs for human participants, but the reinforcement-learning, recurrent-model, and language-model adapters would each need a matching bridge to read its stimulus stream and inject responses. None of these is a limit of the notation, and generalizing the trial-level interface beyond this battery is a roadmap item.

The second kind is a deliberate boundary of *what Studyflow is for* rather than a missing feature. Studyflow is a specification of the study process and not a stimulus-presentation library, so rendering letters at a fixed retinal angle still requires the assessment battery itself or an external framework reached by URL; the diagram describes which stimulus to show, in what order, under what timing constraint, and what to record, and the pixel-level mechanics are left to the presentation software. Some designs are also intrinsically awkward to express as directed graphs, including adaptive trials, certain Bayesian sequential designs, and ABAB single-subject designs that need feedback, dynamic re-allocation, or open-ended replay; the choreography and message-flow elements reach some of this, and the rest is current research.


Two claims central to the paper remain unvalidated, and we mark them as such. We have not measured the legibility of large process-plus-data diagrams against the protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, and analysis scripts they replace, so the single-source comprehension benefit (R3) is a design goal awaiting a usability study. Adoption is also limited: the tooling ships MIT-licensed and browser-only, but external uptake is a goal, not a result, with the signals we watch for set out in §4.5. Naming these edges is part of the contribution.

## 4.5 Future directions


Sibling BPMN extensions in clinical pathways and other domains emerged because a small number of groups committed to the same notation, and Studyflow's layered design is deliberately set up to make new domain extensions cheap, each one being a single schema file plus optional rendering code.


Two lines of empirical work would strengthen the evidence base. The first is a usability study with cognitive scientists, comparing Studyflow diagrams against the artifacts they replace (protocol PDFs, manuscript flow figures, analysis scripts) to test whether the design measurably reduces effort. The second is a set of demonstrations beyond the single study here: a multi-session longitudinal study, a test-retest design, an MLOps pipeline with an audit and training loop, and a larger human/agent benchmark.

More broadly, experimental science increasingly runs on large datasets and automated pipelines, yet the process that produces a result still lacks the machine-readable footing the data already has. Studyflow is one attempt to give it that footing: a study read, run, and trusted from a single source, rather than a trail of documents about it.

# 5. Methods

This section gives the implementation and specification detail behind the framework: the layered schema that defines the language, the on-disk serialization, the formal grammar, the internal structure of the modeler and runner, and the conventions that make a run reproducible.

## 5.1 The language specification

The Studyflow language is defined once and projected into the format each tool needs. The single source of truth is a versioned LinkML schema [@moxon2025linkml] that fixes the element types, attribute constraints, and validation rules independently of any tool, kept as a copy bundled with the modeler and a standalone canonical copy. Its header declares the prefixes that bind Studyflow to the host standard and the community data models: `bpmn` for the BPMN metamodel, `studyflow` and `cognitive` for the two always-loaded layers, and `bids`, `psychds`, `bdm`, and `csvw` for the data bindings. Keeping the specification in LinkML rather than in the modeler codebase is what makes the notation tool-independent, so a third-party linter, converter, or execution engine can target the same file the modeler tracks.

The runtime tooling reads a mirror of that source in the format the BPMN engine expects: the browser's BPMN library consumes moddle YAML schemas, so each LinkML definition is mirrored into a moddle layer carrying the same element types and attributes. The vocabulary is partitioned into six layers, enumerated in the modeler's `SCHEMAS` constant with a `core` flag on each, mapping exactly onto the layered set of §2.1. The two core layers are `studyflow` (the study container, events, sequence flows, the base activity, and shared data infrastructure) and its companion `cognitive` layer (cognitive tasks, video-game paradigms, rest periods, questionnaires, instructions, and research gateways). Four optional layers load on demand: a Behaverse cognitive-assessment battery (`behaverse`), a process-orchestration library (`omniprocess`), a data-transformation library for the DataTrove ecosystem (`datatrove`), and an acquisition layer for the OpenBCI Galea VR headset (`galea`), whose `GaleaRecording` variant carries multimodal metadata spanning EEG, EMG, EOG, EDA, PPG, eye tracking, and a head IMU. Only the two core layers have LinkML mirrors; the optional four are moddle schemas alone, which keeps the authoritative core small while letting new domain semantics plug in.

The schemas drive everything downstream, so documentation, validator, and converters are derived rather than hand-maintained: at startup the modeler globs every `*.moddle.yaml` file, force-enables any `core` layer, and converts each into the structures the palette, inspector, and validator read. The element catalog of @tbl-elements and Supplementary Table S1 is generated from the same LinkML source, and the modeler can emit a LinkML instance from a diagram's data elements, each class carrying a `class_uri` back to its Studyflow type. Because one schema generates the interface, the documentation, and the validation, adding an element type or attribute updates all three at once.

## 5.2 The Studyflow grammar

The structural shape of a Studyflow diagram can also be stated as a formal grammar, independent of the file format in which it is stored. A Studyflow diagram is a typed, attributed directed graph $(N, E, T, \tau, \lambda)$ and is considered well-formed when it parses against the grammar. 

**Listing 4.** The Studyflow grammar in EBNF notation. A study is a labeled collection of elements and sequence flows, activity and gateway types, data operations, data elements, and choreography constructs.

```ebnf
/* ========== Top level ========== */
Definitions       ::= Study*
Study             ::= 'Study' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow)*
SubProcess        ::= 'SubProcess' Identifier Attribute* (Element | SequenceFlow | DataAssociation)*
Element           ::= Event | Activity | Gateway | SubProcess
                    | DataObject | DataCatalog | DataStorage | Dataset
                    | Schema | Array | Snapshot

/* ========== Events ========== */
Event             ::= StartEvent | EndEvent
StartEvent        ::= 'StartEvent' Identifier Attribute*    /* may carry consentFormUri */
EndEvent          ::= 'EndEvent' Identifier Attribute*      /* may carry redirectTo, completionCodeType, completionCode */

/* ========== Activities ========== */
Activity              ::= 'Activity' Identifier ActivityAttributeList Choreography?
ActivityAttributeList ::= ActivityType ActivityAttribute*
ActivityType          ::= '@type' ('CognitiveTask' | 'Questionnaire' | 'Instruction' |
                                   'Rest' | 'VideoGame' | 'BehaverseTask' |
                                   'Script' | 'Manual')
ActivityAttribute     ::= Attribute | DataInput | DataOutput | DataOperation

/* ========== Data transformations ========== */
DataOperation      ::= OpClause+
OpClause           ::= '@op' (PrimitiveOp | CompositeOp) DataInput+ DataOutput+
PrimitiveOp        ::= 'Transform' | 'Map' | 'Filter' | 'FlatMap' | 'Reduce' | 'Group'
CompositeOp        ::= 'Compose' PrimitiveOp+

/* ========== Data elements ========== */
DataCatalog        ::= 'DataCatalog' Identifier Attribute*               /* url */
DataStorage        ::= 'DataStorage' Identifier Attribute*               /* persistent physical store */
Dataset            ::= 'Dataset' Identifier Attribute*                   /* catalog, storage, schema, format */
Schema             ::= 'Schema' Identifier Attribute*                    /* format, body */
Array              ::= 'Array' Identifier Attribute*                     /* dataset, schema */
Snapshot           ::= 'Snapshot' Identifier Attribute*                  /* source, version */
DataObject         ::= 'DataObject' Identifier Attribute*                /* may carry state */
DataInput          ::= '@in' NodeRef
DataOutput         ::= '@out' NodeRef

/* ========== Choreography ========== */
Choreography     ::= 'Choreography' Attribute* ParticipantRef+ InitiatingParticipant? MessageFlowList
ParticipantRef   ::= ProcessRef
InitiatingParticipant ::= ParticipantRef
MessageFlowList  ::= MessageFlow*
MessageFlow      ::= 'MessageFlow' Identifier Attribute* ParticipantRef '->' ParticipantRef

/* ========== Gateways ========== */
Gateway          ::= 'Gateway' Identifier GatewayAttribute*
GatewayAttribute ::= GatewayType | Attribute
GatewayType      ::= '@type' ('Random' | 'StratifiedAllocation' | 'Eligibility' |
                              'Exclusive' | 'Parallel' | 'Inclusive' | 'Complex')
SequenceFlow     ::= 'SequenceFlow' Identifier Attribute* NodeRef '->' NodeRef
                                                            /* optional conditionExpression */

/* ========== Common definitions ========== */
Attribute             ::= Identifier Value
ProcessRef            ::= Identifier
NodeRef               ::= Identifier

/* ========== Basic value types ========== */
Boolean    ::= 'true' | 'false'
Value      ::= String | Number | Boolean | Identifier
Number     ::= '-'? ( [0-9]+ ('.' [0-9]*)? | '.' [0-9]+ )
String     ::= '"' [^"]* '"'
Identifier ::= [A-Za-z] [A-Za-z0-9_]*
```

## 5.3 Serialization

A Studyflow file on disk is a valid BPMN 2.0 XML document in which every element is a standard BPMN element whose payload resides in an `extensionElements` block, so the structure a generic BPMN tool expects is untouched.

This extension mechanism is what makes compatibility a property of the format rather than a feature of any one reader. A generic BPMN reader ignores the extension content it does not recognize and still draws a correct process diagram, while a supported tool reads, validates, and renders the extension blocks. This is BPMN's standard extension protocol [@stroppi2011], so each reader interprets the elements it cares about. The study root marks itself with a `studyflow:study` element inside the root process's `extensionElements`, which lets a Studyflow-aware tool recognize the file as a study without changing how a generic tool treats the underlying `bpmn:process`.

Two further serialization conventions support the design goals. First, Studyflow leaves XML namespaces, element identifiers, and the base vocabulary untouched, so a diagram produces clean line-based diffs in Git and stays valid BPMN. Second, files are saved with a `.studyflow.svg` extension with Studyflow metadata embedded in the SVG (rather than a `.xml` or `.bpmn` extension), so the file that runs the experiment is also the figure that goes in the paper. A single committed file is at once the publication figure and the runnable, diffable source. The same file can be exported to other formats, but the `.studyflow.svg` file is the source of truth.


# Code and data availability

All artifacts are open source under the MIT license and run in the browser without installation. The modeler, runner, and corresponding documentation are hosted at [behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler/app), and the source codes are available at [github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler](https://github.com/behaverse/studyflow-modeler). The canonical schema is versioned separately at [github.com/behaverse/schemas](github.com/behaverse/schemas). The versions used in this paper are tagged in the repository.

Example diagrams referenced in the paper ship with the modeler: a CONSORT 2025-style randomized trial, a SPIRIT 2025 schedule of enrolment and assessment, a base demo, and three agent-profiling demos (`bot_external.studyflow`, a randomized baseline; `bot_claude.studyflow`, a commercial language model; and `bot_ollama.studyflow`, a local open-weight model). Reproducing every figure requires opening the corresponding diagram in the hosted modeler and exporting SVG. Runner figures are reproduced by loading the same files into the runner with seed 42. Permanent links to the exact source commits will be added to the camera-ready version.

Every element specializes a standard BPMN type, given in the *BPMN base* column, so a diagram remains valid BPMN 2.0 and degrades gracefully in a generic BPMN tool. Four optional domain layers (a cognitive assessment battery, a generic process orchestration layer, a large-scale data transformation layer, and a multimodal acquisition layer for EEG and eye tracking) add further specialized elements that plug in without changing the core. The element types, their attributes, and validation rules are generated from the versioned LinkML schema, which is the authoritative source.

Every element also inherits `documentation` and `checklist` attributes from a shared `Element` mixin. The catalog additionally defines enumerations used by these attributes, including dataset formats (BDM, BIDS, Psych-DS, CSVW), BDM data levels, completion-code types, runtimes, assignment algorithms, and instrument identifiers.
